opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think of singular learning theory as the broader foundation. SLT is a mathematical theory of learning in models like neural networks, where the map from parameters to functions is highly degenerate. It tells you things about the geometry of the loss landscape, about which solutions Bayesian learning prefers, about generalization, and it gives you quantities like the learning coefficient that measure the effective complexity of a model. You can apply that toolkit to alignment in many ways: understanding inductive biases, thinking about how models generalize out of distribution, maybe eventually saying something about whether training will select deceptive or misaligned solutions.

Developmental interpretability is one particular research agenda that sits on top of that foundation. The core bet is that to understand what a trained neural network is doing, you should study how it got there, the developmental process over training, rather than only looking at the final snapshot. The hypothesis is that development isn't smooth and uniform but is organized into stages, with phase transitions where the model reorganizes its internal structure and picks up a new capability or algorithm. If you can detect those transitions and localize them, in time and ideally in which components of the network are changing, you get a natural way to carve the model up into meaningful pieces.

SLT is what makes that more than an analogy. It predicts that Bayesian learning moves between regions of parameter space with different tradeoffs between loss and complexity, and those transitions show up as changes in quantities like the local learning coefficient. So we can use estimators like the LLC as a kind of microscope, tracking how complexity changes during training and flagging when something structurally interesting is happening.

So the distinction is roughly: SLT for alignment is the whole program of using this theory to understand learning and generalization, while developmental interpretability is the specific claim that the developmental lens, stages, transitions, and how structure forms, is the right way to do interpretability, with SLT supplying the theory and the tools. In practice they blur together, since a lot of what we've learned building devinterp tools feeds back into the broader agenda, but that's how I'd draw the line.

r001.rationale: It presents loss-landscape geometry and learning-coefficient changes as signals of structural changes in a model, linking them to how the network’s internal structure forms.

r002.rationale: It describes developmental interpretability as using SLT tools such as the LLC to track changes in complexity during training and flag structural transitions.

r003.rationale: It does not identify testing whether SLT’s Bayesian developmental predictions transfer to SGD training.

r004.rationale: It does not state that changing the evaluation-data distribution for a fixed model changes local loss geometry in ways expected to correlate with its mode of computation.

r005.rationale: It does not propose probing a fixed model’s loss geometry across data distributions as an approach to out-of-distribution generalization that avoids tracing training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of them as nested. Singular learning theory is the underlying mathematics. It's a theory of Bayesian statistics for models where the map from parameters to functions isn't one-to-one, which is basically every neural network. It tells you that the geometry of the loss landscape, and in particular these singularities where many parameters implement the same function, controls what the model learns and how it generalizes. That's a general framework, and you can imagine lots of ways of applying it to alignment: understanding generalization, understanding inductive biases, maybe eventually making statements about what kind of structure gradient descent is going to find.

Developmental interpretability is one specific research program that's downstream of that. The bet is that if you want to understand the structure inside a trained network, the right place to look is at how that structure forms over the course of training. Training isn't one smooth process; it goes through phases, and in the SLT picture those phase transitions correspond to the posterior jumping between different regions of the loss landscape with different local complexity. So instead of taking a fully trained model and trying to reverse-engineer billions of parameters at once, you watch the model develop, you locate the transitions, and you try to understand each piece of structure at the moment it appears, when it's still comparatively simple and isolated.

So SLT is the theory, and developmental interpretability is the attempt to turn that theory into actual tools, things like estimating the local learning coefficient along a training trajectory to detect those transitions. You could do developmental interpretability without SLT, and people sort of have, with things like grokking and induction head formation. And you could use SLT for alignment in ways that aren't about development at all. But I think the two fit together naturally, because SLT is precisely a theory that predicts phase transitions should happen and gives you quantities to measure around them.

r001.rationale: The response says loss-landscape geometry controls what a network learns and generalizes, and frames developmental interpretability as studying the structure inside trained networks.

r002.rationale: It describes using SLT to track phase transitions and local complexity over training, including estimating the local learning coefficient along a training trajectory.

r003.rationale: It does not identify testing whether SLT’s Bayesian developmental predictions transfer to SGD training as a research question.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss changes in a fixed model’s local loss geometry across evaluation data distributions or relate them to changes in computation.

r005.rationale: It does not propose probing a fixed model’s loss geometry across data distributions to study out-of-distribution generalization without tracing training.

astra-6.text:
I think of developmental interpretability as a particular research program within the broader application of singular learning theory to alignment. The central idea is that, to understand a neural network, we should study how its structure emerges during training, rather than only examining the finished model. What capabilities appear, when do they appear, and what changes in the model accompany that emergence?

Singular learning theory gives us a mathematical framework for investigating that, especially changes in the effective complexity of what a model has learned. But developmental interpretability isn’t synonymous with singular learning theory: we can use other theoretical and empirical tools to study development, and singular learning theory could have alignment applications beyond interpretability.

So one is a research agenda about understanding models through their development, and the other is a theoretical framework that we hope can help with that agenda, as well as with broader questions about learning and generalization.

r002.rationale: It describes studying how structure emerges during training, but does not characterize the work as studying changes in local loss geometry over training.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Bayesian developmental predictions or whether they transfer to SGD training.

r004.rationale: It does not state that changing the evaluation data distribution can alter a fixed model’s local loss geometry in ways expected to correlate with its mode of computation.

r005.rationale: The response does not identify probing a fixed model’s loss geometry across data distributions as an approach to out-of-distribution generalization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of developmental interpretability as a particular research agenda within the broader project of applying singular learning theory to alignment. The idea is to understand how a model acquires its internal structure over the course of training: when new capabilities or computational mechanisms emerge, and how those transitions happen. So rather than only taking a trained model and asking what it’s doing, we’re also asking how it came to do that.

Singular learning theory gives us a mathematical framework for studying learning in models where many different parameter settings can represent the same function, and where the geometry is more complicated than classical statistical theory assumes. We hope that framework can help us characterize stages of learning and transitions between them.

But its potential relevance to alignment is broader than developmental interpretability. You could use it to study generalization, model selection, or the inductive biases of training—questions that matter for alignment without necessarily telling you what internal mechanisms a model develops. Developmental interpretability is the part that tries to connect that theory to a concrete account of how those mechanisms form.
